title: Batch vs Stream Processing
subtitle: Watch one shop's click events get turned into hourly revenue two ways, and see what each way costs you.
learn: How a MapReduce-style batch job splits, shuffles and reduces a big dataset
How a stream processor keeps running state and emits results continuously
What tumbling, sliding and session windows are and when to use each
Why late events happen and how watermarks decide when a window closes
How lambda and kappa architectures trade complexity for freshness and simplicity

steps.title: Same events, two ways to answer
steps.body: A shop's site and apps emit about 5,000 events per second (clicks, carts, orders). That is roughly 430 million a day, or about 215 GB at 500 bytes each. The business wants revenue per hour on a dashboard. Do you let data pile up and crunch it in big jobs, or process each event the moment it arrives?
steps.idea: Batch processes a finished pile of data; stream processes data that never finishes.
steps.caption: Events flow from sources into a durable log.

steps.title: Batch: collect, then compute
steps.body: Batch works on a bounded dataset: a fixed set of files with a known start and end. Here the log is copied into a data lake as hourly files. Nothing is computed yet, the data just accumulates. Because the input is complete and unchanging, a failed job can simply be rerun on the same files and give the same answer.
steps.idea: A bounded input is finished and repeatable, so reruns are safe and simple.
steps.caption: Events are archived as hourly files.

steps.title: MapReduce: split, shuffle, reduce
steps.body: Once an hour closes, the batch job reads that hour's files, about 9 GB at 500 bytes an event, and cuts them into 128 MB splits, roughly 70 pieces. Map tasks run in parallel on those splits and emit (hour, amount) pairs. The shuffle moves all pairs with the same key to one reducer, and each reducer sums its keys. Results land in the serving store. Modern engines such as Spark use the same split, shuffle, aggregate model. The job starts only after the hour closes, so the dashboard runs over an hour behind.
steps.idea: Batch scales by running many independent map tasks, then grouping by key; its cost is waiting.
steps.caption: Parallel map and reduce tasks write hourly totals.

steps.title: Stream: compute as events arrive
steps.body: A stream processor reads the log continuously and treats the input as unbounded: it never ends, so there is no final answer, only a running one. It keeps state in memory, such as a running sum per hour, updates it on every event, and pushes fresh totals to the serving store. The dashboard is now a couple of seconds behind instead of an hour.
steps.idea: Streaming trades the simplicity of finished input for results that are seconds old.
steps.caption: Each event updates running totals immediately.

steps.title: Windows: cutting an endless stream
steps.body: To get an hourly number from a stream you group events into windows. A tumbling window is fixed and non-overlapping, like each clock hour. A sliding window overlaps, such as the last hour recomputed every 5 minutes, so each event lands in 12 windows. A session window groups one user's activity and closes after a gap, say 30 quiet minutes.
steps.idea: Pick the window shape from the question: fixed buckets, rolling view, or per-user activity.
steps.caption: The processor groups events into windows by time.

steps.title: Late events and watermarks
steps.body: A phone loses signal and sends an order stamped 10:58 only at 11:03. Windows should use event time (when it happened), not processing time (when it arrived), or this order lands in the wrong hour. But the processor needs a rule for when a window is done. A watermark says 'I assume no event older than this is still coming', often the newest event time minus a fixed delay, such as 2 minutes. Anything later is dropped, sent to a side output, or used to correct the result.
steps.idea: A watermark is a guess about completeness: shorter waits give faster results but more late drops.
steps.caption: The order arrives after the 10:00-11:00 window closed.

steps.title: Lambda: run both side by side
steps.body: Early on, stream results were approximate and could be lost, so teams ran two paths over the same events. A speed layer (stream) gives quick but rough numbers. A batch layer recomputes accurate numbers later and overwrites them. The serving store merges the two. It works, but you now write, test and debug the same business logic twice, in two systems, and the results must agree.
steps.idea: Lambda buys accuracy plus speed at the price of maintaining two codebases that must match.
steps.caption: Batch and stream both write into one serving store.

steps.title: Kappa: one stream, replay for fixes
steps.body: Modern stream engines handle state, checkpoints and event time well, so kappa drops the batch path. The log is the source of truth and keeps data for days or months. To fix a bug or change logic, deploy the new version, replay the log from the earliest offset (the start of the log) into a new output table, then switch readers to it. A batch is just a stream that ends. The catch is retention: replay only works if the log still holds the history.
steps.idea: Kappa keeps one codebase by treating reprocessing as a replay of the log.
steps.caption: New code replays the log from offset 0.

steps.title: The stream job crashes
steps.body: The processor dies at 11:20 with 20 minutes of running totals in memory. A batch task would just rerun. A stream job instead takes periodic checkpoints: a snapshot of its state plus the log offset (position) it had reached, say every minute. On restart it reloads the last checkpoint and re-reads from that offset. Some events are processed twice, so the output write must be idempotent (safe to repeat) or transactional to avoid double counting.
steps.idea: Checkpoint plus replay recovers a stream job; idempotent output keeps the replay from double counting.
steps.caption: The job restores a checkpoint and re-reads the log.

steps.title: Choosing between them
steps.body: Use batch when freshness of hours is fine and you need cheap, repeatable crunching of huge history, such as nightly reports or model training. Use stream when decisions need seconds, such as fraud checks or live dashboards. Streams need windows, event time and watermarks to cope with endless, out-of-order input. As a rule of thumb, prefer one codebase over lambda when your engine can replay the log or run the same code in batch mode.
steps.idea: Choose by how stale an answer you can tolerate, then pay for the extra machinery only if you need it.
steps.caption: Batch is simple and hours old; stream is seconds old and needs more care.

quiz.q: An order happened at 10:58 on a phone with no signal and reached the stream processor at 11:03. Why should hourly windows use event time here?
options: Event time is always faster to compute
It removes the need for a log
The order belongs to the 10:00-11:00 hour, and arrival time would put it in the wrong one
Processing time cannot be used with windows
quiz.why: Event time records when something actually happened, so results stay correct despite delays. Processing time would count the order in 11:00-12:00 and change results whenever the pipeline is slow.

quiz.q: What is the main ongoing cost of a lambda architecture?
options: The log cannot store more than a day of data
The same business logic must be written and kept consistent in a batch system and a stream system
Batch jobs cannot read from the data lake
Serving stores cannot accept two writers
quiz.why: Lambda runs two code paths over the same events. Any logic change must be made twice, and the two paths can disagree, which is the main reason teams move to kappa.

quiz.q: Which workload fits batch processing best?
options: Recomputing a product-recommendation model over three years of purchase history each night
Blocking a stolen card within one second of a purchase
A live dashboard of orders in the last minute
Alerting when a sensor reads above a threshold
quiz.why: Large, bounded history with no need for second-level freshness is where batch is cheapest and simplest. The other three need results in seconds.

quiz.q: You find a bug in a kappa pipeline's revenue logic from last week. What is the sound fix?
options: Patch the running job and accept that last week's numbers stay wrong
Delete the log and wait for new events
Convert the pipeline to lambda immediately
Deploy the fixed job, replay the log from the needed offset into a new output, then switch readers to it
quiz.why: Kappa treats reprocessing as replay. This works only if the log's retention still covers the affected period, so retention is a design decision.

cheatsheet.def: Bounded data has a known end (a day's files), so batch can finish. Unbounded data never ends (live events), so stream jobs run forever.
Map tasks process input splits in parallel and emit key/value pairs; the shuffle groups equal keys; reduce tasks combine each group's values.
Fixed-size, non-overlapping buckets, such as each clock hour. Every event belongs to exactly one window.
Fixed size but advancing in smaller steps (1 hour every 5 minutes). Windows overlap, so each event counts in several.
Groups one key's events until a gap of inactivity (for example 30 minutes). Length varies per user.
Event time is when it happened; processing time is when the system sees it. Use event time for correct results under delays.
A moving estimate that no earlier events are still coming, often newest event time minus a fixed delay. It closes windows; later events are dropped or handled separately.
Lambda runs batch and stream paths and merges them. Kappa uses only a stream over a replayable log and reprocesses by replaying.
